title: Fewest Rolls on a Chutes Board
statement:
A square board board has n × n cells numbered 1 to n². Numbering starts at the bottom-left cell and runs left to right along the bottom row, then right to left along the row above, and keeps zig-zagging upward. So board[n − 1][0] is cell 1.

A cell value of -1 means a plain cell. Any other value v is a chute or a ladder: landing on that cell by a roll moves you straight to cell v.

You start on cell 1. Each turn, roll a die and choose any result from 1 to 6: move from cell c to cell c + roll (never past n²). If you land on a chute or ladder, follow it, but only once per turn: if its destination starts another one, you do not follow that second one.

Return the fewest turns needed to reach cell n², or -1 if it cannot be reached.

examples.why: No jumps. From 1, a roll of 6 reaches 7, then a roll of 2 reaches 9.
board[2][1] is cell 2. Roll a 1 and climb straight to 9.
Cell 2 leads to 8, and cell 8 (board[2][0]) leads to 16. Rolling to 2 stops on 8, since jumps do not chain. Instead roll 6 to cell 7, then roll 1 onto cell 8 and climb to 16.

constraints: board[i][j] is -1 or between 1 and n²
hints: Every turn costs the same, so "fewest turns" is a shortest path in an unweighted graph. Which algorithm gives that directly?
Nodes are cell numbers 1..n². From cell c there are up to six edges: to c + 1 … c + 6, each redirected if that cell holds a jump.
The fiddly part is turning a cell number into (row, col): row = n − 1 − ⌊(c − 1) / n⌋, and the column runs forward on even rows from the bottom, backward on odd ones.

explain.intuition:
Ignore the grid for a moment. The game is a graph on cells 1 to n², where each cell has up to six outgoing edges, and every edge costs one turn. The fewest turns from cell 1 to cell n² is a shortest path in an unweighted graph, which breadth-first search finds level by level.

The grid only matters for one thing: finding which cell of board holds the jump for cell number c. Count rows from the bottom with (c − 1) / n; even rows from the bottom run left to right and odd rows run right to left.
steps: Write cellAt(c): q = ⌊(c − 1) / n⌋, row = n − 1 − q, col = (c − 1) % n, and mirror col to n − 1 − col when q is odd.
BFS from cell 1 with distance 0, marking cells as visited.
For the current cell c, try every next from c + 1 to min(c + 6, n²). If board holds a jump there, replace next by its destination.
If next is n², return the current distance + 1. Otherwise queue it if it is unvisited.
pitfalls: Getting the zig-zag wrong, for example by mirroring the column on even rows counted from the top. It only shows on boards with an even size.
Following a chain of jumps in one turn. Each roll follows at most one jump.
Marking the cell you rolled onto as visited instead of the jump's destination. The BFS state is where you end the turn.

solutions.title: Relax until nothing changes
solutions.idea: Keep a best-turns value per cell and repeatedly sweep all cells, improving neighbours, until a sweep makes no change.

solutions.title: BFS over cell numbers
solutions.idea: Each turn is one BFS level. The first time cell n² is reached, the level number is the answer.

followups: Return the actual sequence of rolls, not just the count.
The die is now fair and random. What is the expected number of turns? (Hint: a system of linear equations, or value iteration.)
